analysis.one_liner: Taxes the windfall profits of big crude oil companies and sends the money back as gasoline-price rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond a committee referral; it received no markup and no vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted or imported by large oil companies (those handling over 300,000 barrels a day), charged only on the amount that quarterly Brent crude prices exceed their pre-pandemic 2015-2019 average. All of the money collected would go into a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and be paid out as quarterly, refundable rebates to individuals, phasing down for higher incomes. It was introduced in March 2022, when gasoline prices were at record highs, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers hit by high gasoline prices in 2022. Individuals would receive quarterly rebate checks from the fund, with married couples getting 150% of the single rate and the rebate phasing down above $75,000 of income ($112,500 for heads of household, $150,000 for joint filers). Lower- and middle-income people, who spend a larger share of income on fuel, would keep the full rebate.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted in or imported into the United States by large producers and importers, applied to the amount by which quarterly average Brent crude prices exceed their 2015-2019 average, with the threshold adjusted for inflation after 2022.

The tax applies only to large companies — those extracting and importing more than 300,000 barrels of crude per day in 2019 or in the current quarter — and treats affiliated companies as one for the threshold.
All revenue collected goes into a Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund, and the bill requires the tax collected to be rebated to individual taxpayers.

The rebate is a refundable credit paid quarterly, at 150% of the standard amount for joint filers, phasing down by 5% of income above $75,000 ($112,500 head of household, $150,000 joint), so it reaches low- and middle-income households in full.

The bill includes advance refunds quarterly within 90 days, an IRS outreach program, payments to U.S. territories so residents benefit, and protection of the rebates from being offset against other federal debts.

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers and importers, which would pay the excise tax out of their windfall profits during price spikes. Some of the tax could also be passed to consumers at the pump in the form of higher fuel prices, and economists generally note windfall taxes can reduce investment incentive in domestic drilling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big crude oil producers and importers

drawbacks.text: Because the tax is levied on each barrel of crude rather than on accounting profits, companies can be expected to pass at least part of it to consumers in higher gasoline prices, which would eat into the rebate the bill provides.

The tax is keyed to a fixed price benchmark — Brent crude averaged over 2015-2019, adjusted for inflation — rather than to what a company actually earns, so it can be owed even in periods when a particular producer is not earning windfall profits and may reduce incentives to increase domestic oil output.

The rebate machinery is complex: quarterly IRS determinations, advance-refund rules keyed to prior-year returns, and identification-number requirements for non-filers mean real administrative burden and possible missed payments for the lowest-income people it is meant to reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and the design is pointed: it reaches into windfall profits that only a few dozen very large companies would pay and routes every dollar to consumers as quarterly cash, with full amounts going to those least able to absorb high gas prices. The honest costs are that part of the tax likely lands back on pump prices — partially offsetting the rebate — and that a barrel-based tax on a price benchmark rather than on actual profits is a blunt instrument that can hit producers who are not earning windfalls. On balance, the consumer-side benefits were the bill's main purpose and the costs fall mostly on a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2022 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it received no markup and no vote and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill in the House on March 11, 2022, during the period of record-high gasoline prices.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over excise taxes.
Twenty-four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred — only the introduction and the referral.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large crude oil producers and importers, which kept their 2022 windfall profits untaxed, and higher-income consumers, who would have borne little of the tax but were phased out of the rebate. Everyday consumers received no relief checks because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil kept windfall profits untaxed

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on March 11, 2022 and sponsored it through the end of the Congress.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote; it sat in committee from March 2022 until the Congress expired, per the action history.

against.name: Major oil and gas companies and their trade groups
against.role: Industry whose windfall profits the bill would tax
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed windfall-profit taxes on oil companies during the 2022 price spike, arguing such taxes would discourage investment in domestic production.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it; the committee that declined to move it was chaired by a Democrat, so support was entirely within one party.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: The bill would take 50% of the difference between quarterly world oil prices and their pre-2020 norm on every barrel these companies extract or import — money that in 2022 flowed to shareholders and executives during record pump prices. The industry's interest in keeping that revenue runs directly against the consumer relief the bill funds.

The tax falls upstream on crude extraction and imports, not on stations, though retailers would face whatever portion of the tax producers pass forward into fuel prices. Consumer rebates would support fuel demand during price spikes.
